texto.nota: Texto fictício, escrito para estudo no formato de um artigo de revisão. Autores, periódico, citações, estudos e dados numéricos são inventados; os conceitos descritos (controle executivo, inibição, alternância, atualização da memória de trabalho, tarefas Flanker, Simon, Stroop e de alternância de tarefas, viés de publicação, pré-registro, metanálise bayesiana) são gerais.
texto.periodico: Journal of Language and Cognitive Inquiry (2024) 12(3), 201–236
texto.titulo: Advantage, effect or artefact? Bilingualism, executive control and the problem of replication
texto.abstract: This article reviews the debate over whether the regular use of two languages enhances executive control, and in particular the ability to inhibit irrelevant information. It begins with the need for rigour in a field whose claims have been widely publicised, and then compares how executive control and bilingualism have been defined, arguing that much of the disagreement originates in the definition of bilingualism rather than in that of executive control. The origins of the ‘bilingual advantage’ hypothesis are traced, and the methodological problems that have accompanied it – small samples, publication bias, socioeconomic and immigration confounds and vague group definitions – are evaluated in the light of large-sample replications and meta-analyses. Proposals to redefine the question are then considered, together with five means by which it may be tested. It is argued that the question of whether bilinguals outperform monolinguals is poorly posed, and that it should be reformulated as the question of which features of language experience, in which contexts of use, are associated with which components of executive control.
texto.keywords: bilingualism, executive control, inhibition, replication, publication bias, meta-analysis

blocos.h2: 1. The need for rigour in research on bilingualism and cognition

blocos.p: It is now widely accepted that claims about the cognitive consequences of language experience must be held to the same evidential standards as any other claim in experimental psychology. For the proposition that bilingualism enhances executive control, those standards may be stated as a set of minimal conditions: that effects be estimated in samples large enough to detect them reliably; that bilingual and monolingual groups be matched on socioeconomic status and immigration history; that ‘bilingual’ be defined by stated thresholds of age of acquisition, proficiency and frequency of use; that the tasks employed be shown to measure the control process they are said to measure; and that results be reported whether or not they favour the hypothesis. Few of the studies published before 2010 met more than two of these conditions (Kessling and Yuen 2016). Several responses to this situation can be identified: declaring the advantage a myth and abandoning the question altogether; accepting the advantage as established and attributing null results to insensitive measurement; retaining the question while redefining both of its terms, so that bilingualism is treated as a set of graded experiences and executive control as a family of separable processes; and replacing it with a broader inquiry into the effects of any sustained cognitive activity, of which language use would be only one instance. It is the third of these which is defended here.

The need for such conditions is not merely academic. Few findings in the psychology of language have travelled as far beyond the laboratory: the claim that speaking two languages ‘trains the brain’ has been invoked in debates over heritage-language schooling, in advice offered to the parents of migrant children and in the marketing of language-learning products to older adults (Nakashima-Rowe 2018). An unwarranted claim of advantage risks raising expectations that families and schools cannot meet; an unwarranted claim of no advantage risks being read as evidence that a bilingual upbringing is without value, which is a separate question altogether. Since the communicative, cultural and economic benefits of knowing two languages do not depend on any executive bonus, the debate reviewed here concerns a narrow empirical proposition and should not be mistaken for a referendum on bilingualism itself. It is precisely because the proposition is narrow that it can, in principle, be tested. Public interest has also shaped the literature itself: a finding that confirms a popular claim is more likely to attract press coverage, citations and funding than one that does not, and researchers are not immune to these incentives. A field in which positive results are rewarded twice over, once by journals and once by the public, has particular reason to adopt the safeguards listed above.

Definitions of executive control vary less than definitions of bilingualism, but they are not interchangeable. Halloran-Petit (2004, p. 17) describes it as ‘the set of general-purpose processes that regulate thought and action in the service of a currently held goal’, a formulation which emphasises its domain-general character. Okonkwo-Lindahl (2009, p. 212) adopts a componential view, distinguishing inhibition, the suppression of dominant but inappropriate responses; switching, the shifting of attention between tasks or mental sets; and updating, the monitoring and revision of the contents of working memory. These components are, in her account, ‘correlated but separable’, so that an improvement in one need not be accompanied by an improvement in the others. Draven-Saito (2011, p. 45) narrows the term still further, treating inhibitory control as the core of executive function and defining it as ‘the ability to withhold a prepotent response or to ignore information that competes with the goal’. It is this last definition that underlies most of the early literature on bilingualism, which explains why the debate has been conducted largely in terms of inhibition.

The componential view has an inconvenient implication for research on bilingualism. No task measures a single component in isolation: a Stroop task, in which the participant names the ink colour of a word that may denote a different colour, requires inhibition, but also sustained attention, reading skill and processing speed. This ‘task impurity problem’ is usually addressed by computing difference scores, such as the extra time needed on incongruent relative to congruent trials, on the assumption that the general demands of the task cancel out. Difference scores, however, are notoriously unreliable: Feldt-Arango (2020) reports test–retest correlations between .20 and .45 for the interference effects of four commonly used tasks, against .80 or more for the overall response times from which they were derived. A measure that does not correlate with itself across two sessions is unlikely to correlate with language background, and a group difference in such a measure is correspondingly difficult to interpret.

Definitions of bilingualism range from the inclusive to the exacting. Szabo-Ferreira (1998, p. 3) proposes that bilinguals are ‘those who use two or more languages, or dialects, in their everyday lives’, a definition which makes regular use, rather than level of mastery, the criterion. Marquand-Oduya (2006, p. 88), by contrast, reserves the term for speakers with ‘native-like control of two languages’, acquired, in most cases, before adolescence. Between these poles, Tavares-Lund (2013, p. 140) argues that bilingualism is not a category but ‘a multidimensional continuum of experience’, on which individuals are located by age of acquisition, proficiency in each language and the proportion of daily life conducted in each. Ibekwe-Castell (2016, p. 59) adds a dimension the others ignore: the interactional context, distinguishing speakers who use each language in separate settings, those who use both in the same settings but with different interlocutors, and those who habitually mix languages within a single conversation.

The practical consequence of this diversity is that the ‘bilingual’ and ‘monolingual’ groups of different studies are often not comparable. In a survey of 118 studies published between 2004 and 2019, Petrakis-Ndlovu (2019) found that only 41 reported the age at which the second language had been acquired, 29 reported an objective measure of proficiency and just 12 reported how often each language was used; the remainder classified participants on the basis of a single self-report question. Several ‘monolingual’ groups included participants who had studied a second language at school for six years or more, while some ‘bilingual’ groups included heritage speakers who could understand but not speak the family language. Where two studies reach opposite conclusions, it is therefore impossible to know whether they disagree about the effect of bilingualism or are simply measuring different populations. Petrakis-Ndlovu does not conclude that the earlier studies are worthless, but that their results cannot be pooled without first being re-coded according to a common set of language-background variables.

Dissatisfaction with the category has led to a proliferation of qualified labels. ‘Balanced bilingual’, ‘active bilingual’, ‘functional bilingual’ and ‘early bilingual’ have all been proposed as more precise alternatives, each intended to pick out the subgroup in which an advantage might reasonably be expected (Corvino-Haas 2017). Some accounts, however, offer no explanation of how the new label differs from the old. ‘Functional bilingual’, for instance, is defined in one widely used protocol simply as ‘a person who can function in two languages’, which restates the inclusive definition without adding a threshold. Other labels conceal a threshold that is never stated: a participant may be ‘balanced’ if her self-rated proficiency differs by less than one point between languages on a seven-point scale, or by less than two, depending on the laboratory, and two studies of ‘balanced bilinguals’ may accordingly be studying quite different people. Multiplying labels in this way gives an appearance of precision while leaving the underlying variables unmeasured. What is required is not a better name for the group but a record of the experiences that place each individual within it.

The hypothesis rests on a well-supported observation about bilingual language processing: both languages are active even when only one is being used. Evidence for this joint activation comes from studies showing that words in the non-target language influence recognition and production times in the target language, even in tasks that never require the non-target language to be used (Rennick-Abara 2004). If both languages compete for selection, the bilingual speaker must continually suppress the one not in use, and must do so many thousands of times a day. It was reasoned that such sustained practice might strengthen the general inhibitory mechanism on which language control was assumed to draw, in the same way that physical exercise strengthens a muscle that serves many different movements. The argument thus links a specific linguistic demand to a domain-general benefit, and its plausibility depends on the assumption that language control and non-linguistic inhibition share the same underlying mechanism.

The first studies appeared to confirm the prediction. Rennick-Abara (2004) reported that 32 bilingual children responded faster than 32 monolingual peers on the incongruent trials of a Simon task, and similar results were soon reported for young adults and, most strikingly, for older adults, among whom the advantage seemed larger than at any other age (Ostrova-Diallo 2007). Effect sizes in this early literature were frequently large, with standardised differences of 0.6 or more, and samples rarely exceeded 40 participants per group. In retrospect, this combination ought itself to have prompted caution, since small samples can produce large estimated effects by chance, and only those estimates that reach significance tend to be published. Few of these early studies were designed to detect effects smaller than d = 0.5, and none, so far as can be determined, specified its analyses in advance; both features would later prove important. Even so, the findings were consistent with a coherent theoretical account, and their consistency was taken as corroboration.

Doubts were first raised not by a failed replication but by an audit of conference abstracts. Kessling and Yuen (2016) traced 104 abstracts on bilingualism and executive control presented at meetings between 1999 and 2012 and found that 63% of those reporting a clear advantage had subsequently been published in full, compared with 31% of those reporting null or mixed results. Because the abstracts had been accepted at the same meetings, differences in quality could not easily explain the gap. The authors also documented the tendency of smaller studies to report larger effects, a pattern which is expected when significant results are selectively published, and estimated that, once this asymmetry was corrected for, the mean advantage across 152 published comparisons fell from d = 0.30 to d = 0.04, a value statistically indistinguishable from zero.

A second difficulty concerns what else differs between bilingual and monolingual groups. In many of the countries where the early studies were conducted, bilingual participants were disproportionately drawn from immigrant families, and immigration is itself selective: those who migrate tend to differ from those who stay in education, health and motivation, and these differences may be transmitted to their children. Socioeconomic status presents the opposite problem, since in other settings bilingual children more often come from low-income households, which would be expected to mask any advantage rather than produce one. Morland-Achebe (2014) showed that, in a sample of 1,240 primary-school children, a bilingual advantage on a flanker task of d = 0.25 disappeared once parental education and immigrant generation were entered as covariates, whereas it was unaffected by controlling for age and sex. Matching on these variables is not straightforward, because in some communities there are almost no monolingual children of immigrant background with whom bilingual children can be compared.

The most direct test came from studies large enough to detect effects of the size reported in the early literature. Varhaug, Szalai and Osei (2015) administered flanker, Simon and task-switching tasks online to 2,140 adults aged 18 to 35, of whom 712 reported regular use of two or more languages, and found no difference between the groups on any interference or switch-cost measure. Proponents objected that their participants had been classified by a single question and tested on home computers, under conditions that could not be controlled. These objections were partly met by Lindholm-Amaro (2018), who tested 486 children in schools using identical equipment and a detailed language-background interview, and who also reported no reliable effect. Two subsequent meta-analyses reached compatible conclusions: when the analyses were restricted to studies with at least 100 participants per group, the pooled effect was close to zero, and its confidence interval excluded the values reported in the studies that had first established the hypothesis.

Defenders of the hypothesis have offered three replies. The first is that the tasks are too easy for healthy young adults, whose performance is close to ceiling, so that an advantage would be expected only in children and older adults, in whom executive control is still developing or already declining. The second is that the advantage lies not in inhibition but in monitoring, the ability to detect when control is needed, which would show up in overall response times rather than in interference effects (Ostrova-Diallo 2019). The third is that the large studies sampled the wrong bilinguals: people who use their two languages in separate settings, for whom the demands on control are modest. Each reply is reasonable in itself, but each was formulated after the repeated failure of large, internet-based samples of young adults to reproduce the laboratory findings, and none specifies in advance the result that would count against it. If no conceivable result could count against them, in what sense do they remain empirical claims?

The debate has consequently reached a form of impasse. Proponents can point to a substantial body of positive findings, and critics to the evidence that those findings are inflated by bias and confounding. Studies that define bilingualism more carefully have also tended to be larger and better matched. Paradoxically, it is these studies, which ought to have been best placed to reveal an advantage if one existed, that have most consistently failed to find it: in the re-coded data set of Petrakis-Ndlovu (2019), the proportion of comparisons favouring bilinguals fell from 58% among studies using a single self-report question to 17% among those reporting all three language-background variables. For critics, this pattern is decisive; for proponents, it shows only that the wrong variables have been recorded.

A growing number of researchers have concluded that the comparison of ‘bilinguals’ with ‘monolinguals’ is itself the source of the difficulty. If bilingualism is a continuum of experience, as Tavares-Lund (2013) argues, then dividing participants into two groups discards most of the information about them and treats as equivalent individuals whose experience of language control differs greatly. The alternative is to model executive performance as a function of continuous measures – age of acquisition, proficiency in each language, proportion of daily use, frequency of code-switching – and of the contexts in which each language is used. On this view, the question ‘Do bilinguals have an advantage?’ is broken down into a set of narrower questions, each of which specifies the experience, the component of control and the population concerned.

The contextual approach generates predictions that the group comparison cannot. A speaker who uses each language in a separate setting, such as one at home and the other at work, rarely needs to switch within a conversation and should therefore make modest demands on inhibition; a speaker in a dual-language context, who must use the appropriate language with each interlocutor in the same setting, would be expected to rely heavily on monitoring and switching; and a speaker in a dense code-switching community, where mixing is the norm, may need comparatively little inhibition at all. Early tests are encouraging but small. Haverkamp-Iwu (2021) reported that the frequency of switching between interlocutors, but not overall proficiency, predicted smaller switch costs in 160 adults; the finding awaits replication in an independent sample, and the authors themselves describe it as exploratory. Studies of dual-language and code-switching contexts in children and older adults, the two groups in which the evidence remains least settled, have yet to be reported, and it is there that the contextual approach could most usefully be put to the test.

blocos.h2: 7. The means to test the hypothesis

blocos.p: Corvino-Haas (2017) suggests that much of the controversy reflects a confusion between the question being asked and the means by which it may be answered. Once these are separated, five means can be distinguished: the conflict tasks used to estimate inhibitory control, of which the flanker and Simon tasks are the most common; task-switching paradigms, which target the shifting component; language-background questionnaires, which quantify the experience whose effects are sought; pre-registered large-sample studies; and Bayesian meta-analysis, which permits the evidence for and against an effect to be weighed. None is sufficient alone, and each has limitations that the others partly offset. They are discussed below roughly in the order in which they entered the literature, from the conflict tasks of the earliest studies to the statistical methods of the most recent.

In the flanker task, the participant indicates the direction of a central arrow flanked by arrows pointing either the same way (congruent trials) or the opposite way (incongruent trials); in the Simon task, the participant responds to the colour of a stimulus that appears on the same side as, or the opposite side from, the correct response key. In both, the cost of incongruence is taken as an index of the ability to resolve conflict between competing responses (Draven-Saito 2011). Their principal benefit is economy: each takes under ten minutes, can be administered to children and older adults alike and has been used in hundreds of studies, so that new results can be compared directly with old ones. Their limitation is the low reliability of the interference score discussed above, together with the finding that interference effects from the two tasks correlate only weakly with each other (r = .12; Feldt-Arango 2020), which casts doubt on whether they measure a common inhibitory ability.

In task-switching paradigms, participants alternate between two simple tasks, such as classifying a digit by parity or by magnitude, according to a cue that changes unpredictably. The switch cost, the additional time required on trials where the task changes, is assumed to index the shifting component of control, and the mixing cost, the slowing on repeat trials within mixed blocks compared with single-task blocks, is assumed to index monitoring. Because switching between languages appears to resemble switching between tasks more closely than ignoring a flanking arrow does, these paradigms are held to provide a more plausible link between language experience and non-linguistic control (Haverkamp-Iwu 2021). Their limitation is that switch costs depend heavily on the interval between cue and stimulus, so that laboratories using different intervals may obtain results that cannot be compared. Laboratories might usefully agree on a small set of standard intervals, so that switch costs obtained in different studies could at least be placed on a common scale.

Language-background questionnaires record, for each participant, the age at which each language was acquired, self-rated and, in better instruments, tested proficiency, the proportion of each day spent using each language and the settings and interlocutors involved. Their benefit is that they allow bilingualism to be treated as a set of continuous variables rather than as a category and, when the same instrument is used across studies, make results from different populations comparable (Tavares-Lund 2013). Their limitation is that self-reports of language use are imprecise: when Ibekwe-Castell (2016) compared questionnaire estimates with a week of recorded speech from 48 participants, estimates of daily switching frequency were inflated by a factor of two on average, although estimates of the proportion of time spent in each language were reasonably accurate. A practical compromise, lately adopted in several studies, is to combine a short questionnaire with language diaries kept over several days, which adds little to the burden on participants while providing a check on retrospective estimates of switching.

Pre-registration requires the hypotheses, sample size, exclusion criteria and analysis plan to be recorded in a public repository before the data are collected. Combined with samples of several hundred participants per group, it removes the two main sources of inflated estimates in the early literature: the freedom to choose among analyses after seeing the data and the selective publication of significant results, since registered reports are accepted for publication before the outcome is known. Its limitation is cost: a study large enough to detect an effect of d = 0.10 with adequate power requires more than 1,500 participants per group, a number that laboratories testing in person can seldom reach, and multi-site collaborations introduce variation in procedures that must itself be modelled. These costs are not, however, an argument against pre-registration itself, which can be applied to studies of any size; they are an argument for pooling resources across laboratories rather than conducting many small studies, none of which can settle the question on its own.

Conventional meta-analysis estimates the average effect across studies, but a non-significant average does not distinguish between evidence of absence and absence of evidence. Bayesian meta-analysis addresses this by computing a Bayes factor, which expresses how much more probable the data are under the hypothesis of no effect than under the hypothesis of a positive effect, or the reverse (Rask-Okonjo 2022). Applied to 170 comparisons, this approach yielded moderate evidence for the null hypothesis in young adults but inconclusive evidence in children and older adults, a distinction that a conventional analysis would have obscured. The comparisons were not evenly spread across age groups: 58 involved children (4,310 participants), 79 young adults (9,870) and 33 older adults (2,060), with pooled effects of d = 0.08, d = 0.01 and d = 0.11, respectively, against d = 0.04 for all 170 taken together. In none of the three groups does the 95% confidence interval of the pooled effect exclude zero, so that a conventional analysis would have returned the same verdict, no significant effect, for all of them. The Bayes factors, by contrast, separate young adults, for whom the data are almost seven times more probable under the null hypothesis, from children and older adults, for whom neither hypothesis is clearly favoured. The largest point estimate, d = 0.11 in older adults, comes from the fewest comparisons and carries the widest interval; it is better read as a reason to collect more data in that group than as evidence of an advantage. Its limitation is that the Bayes factor depends on the prior distribution assumed for the size of the effect under the alternative hypothesis, so that two analysts using the same data but different priors may reach different conclusions.

There is a clear need for the claim that bilingualism enhances executive control to be held to the evidential standards outlined at the beginning of this article, given how widely it has been publicised. The evidence reviewed here does not support the existence of a general advantage on conflict tasks in young adults, and the larger and better controlled a study has been, the smaller the effect it has tended to report. It does not, however, demonstrate that language experience has no consequences for cognitive control: the evidence for children and older adults remains inconclusive, and contextual measures of language use have barely begun to be tested. In this respect, the contrast between moderate evidence for the null hypothesis in young adults and inconclusive evidence in the other age groups is more informative than either side of the debate has generally acknowledged: it indicates not only where an advantage is unlikely, but also where the question remains open.

The question ‘Are bilinguals better at executive control?’ should therefore be reformulated rather than abandoned: not because the answer is known to be no, but because, in its present form, it is too coarse to be answered. Instead, research should ask which features of language experience, in which contexts of use, are associated with which components of control, and in whom. This requires that bilingualism be measured as a set of continuous experiences, that executive control be measured with tasks of known reliability, and that predictions be registered before the data are collected. The need is not for a new label for the advantage, nor for a final verdict on its existence, but for better-specified questions and the means to answer them.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no título e no resumo, o tema do artigo é
alternativas: o debate sobre se o uso regular de duas línguas aprimora a memória de trabalho, em especial a capacidade de atualizar informações relevantes.
a influência do controle executivo, sobretudo da capacidade de inibição, sobre o modo como os bilíngues usam e alternam suas duas línguas.
a crise de replicação na psicologia experimental, com destaque para o viés de publicação e para as metanálises que o corrigem.
o debate sobre se o uso regular de duas línguas aprimora o controle executivo, em especial a capacidade de inibir informação irrelevante.
o debate sobre se o uso regular de duas línguas traz vantagens cognitivas, comunicativas e econômicas aos filhos de famílias imigrantes.
questoes.explicacao:
O resumo delimita o objeto na primeira frase: the debate over whether the regular use of two languages enhances executive control, and in particular the ability to inhibit irrelevant information. O título repete os eixos (Bilingualism, executive control and the problem of replication). Só (d) mantém os três elementos: o debate, o sentido da relação (uso de duas línguas → controle executivo) e o destaque para a inibição.

(a) troca um único elemento: memória de trabalho (updating) é só um dos componentes do controle executivo citados no §3; o foco declarado é a inibição. (b) inverte a direção: o texto pergunta se o bilinguismo melhora o controle executivo, não como o controle executivo afeta o uso das línguas. (c) é amplo demais: viés de publicação e metanálises aparecem como problemas e meios dentro do debate sobre bilinguismo, não como tema. (e) troca o tipo de benefício e o público: o §2 diz justamente que os benefícios comunicativos, culturais e econômicos não estão em discussão (do not depend on any executive bonus), e o texto não se restringe a filhos de imigrantes.
questoes.dica: Dica: Monte o tema com os elementos do título e da primeira frase do resumo (o quê, em que direção, com que recorte) e confira cada alternativa elemento por elemento. Quando três alternativas começam iguais, o erro está no fim: um componente trocado, um benefício diferente ou um público restrito.

questoes.enunciado: No parágrafo 1, os autores listam as condições mínimas que os estudos sobre bilinguismo e controle executivo deveriam satisfazer. Qual elemento NÃO é citado entre essas condições?
alternativas: Estimar os efeitos em amostras grandes o bastante para detectá-los de modo confiável.
Registrar publicamente as hipóteses e o plano de análise antes da coleta dos dados.
Parear os grupos bilíngue e monolíngue quanto ao nível socioeconômico e ao histórico de imigração.
Definir “bilíngue” por limiares explícitos de idade de aquisição, proficiência e frequência de uso.
Relatar os resultados quer eles favoreçam, quer não favoreçam a hipótese testada.
questoes.explicacao:
A lista vem depois dos dois-pontos de a set of minimal conditions:, com os itens separados por ponto e vírgula e todos introduzidos por that: that effects be estimated in samples large enough to detect them reliably (a); that bilingual and monolingual groups be matched on socioeconomic status and immigration history (c); that ‘bilingual’ be defined by stated thresholds of age of acquisition, proficiency and frequency of use (d); that the tasks employed be shown to measure the control process they are said to measure; e that results be reported whether or not they favour the hypothesis (e).

(b) é o intruso. O registro prévio de hipóteses e do plano de análise é tema do texto, mas aparece só no §21 (Pre-registration requires the hypotheses, sample size, exclusion criteria and analysis plan to be recorded in a public repository before the data are collected), como um dos meios de teste, e não entre as condições do §1. A semelhança com (e), que também trata de viés de publicação, torna a troca tentadora.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em questões de “NÃO”, ache a lista no parágrafo pedido (dois-pontos, ponto e vírgula, uma mesma estrutura repetida como that…; that…) e marque item por item. O intruso costuma ser um assunto do próprio texto, tirado de outra seção, e parecido com um item verdadeiro.

questoes.enunciado: No segmento “It is the third of these which is defended here” (§1), o segmento destacado se refere a
alternativas: “accepting the advantage as established and attributing null results to insensitive measurement” (§1).
“replacing it with a broader inquiry into the effects of any sustained cognitive activity […]” (§1).
“retaining the question while redefining both of its terms […]” (§1).
“Several responses to this situation can be identified” (§1).
“declaring the advantage a myth and abandoning the question altogether” (§1).
questoes.explicacao:
These retoma os itens listados depois de Several responses to this situation can be identified:, separados por ponto e vírgula: (1) declaring the advantage a myth…; (2) accepting the advantage as established…; (3) retaining the question while redefining both of its terms…; (4) replacing it with a broader inquiry…. The third é o terceiro item → (c). A conclusão confirma: a pergunta deve ser reformulated rather than abandoned e medida por variáveis contínuas (§24), o que corresponde a manter a pergunta redefinindo seus dois termos.

(e) é a primeira resposta e (a) a segunda; (b) é a quarta, e é a armadilha de quem lê só a conclusão às pressas, porque ela fala em pôr outra pergunta no lugar (mas o §1 fala em uma investigação mais ampla sobre qualquer atividade cognitiva, e a conclusão pede perguntas mais estreitas). (d) é a frase que introduz a lista, não um de seus itens. Atenção também à outra lista do mesmo parágrafo (as condições mínimas): these retoma a lista mais próxima, a das respostas.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em “the first/second/third of these”, ache a enumeração imediatamente anterior (dois-pontos, ponto e vírgula, mesma forma -ing em cada item) e conte. Se o parágrafo tiver duas listas, a expressão retoma a mais próxima. Confirme com a conclusão do texto, que costuma retomar a posição defendida.

questoes.enunciado:
Nos parágrafos 3 e 5, os autores comparam definições de controle executivo e de bilinguismo. Associe cada autor à ideia que o texto lhe atribui.

  1. Okonkwo-Lindahl (2009)
  2. Draven-Saito (2011)
  3. Szabo-Ferreira (1998)
  4. Tavares-Lund (2013)
  5. Ibekwe-Castell (2016)
  • (  )Situa cada falante em uma escala de várias dimensões, conforme quando aprendeu cada língua, quão bem domina cada uma e quanto do cotidiano vive em cada uma.
  • (  )Considera bilíngue quem usa duas ou mais línguas, ou dialetos, no dia a dia, sem fazer do grau de domínio o critério.
  • (  )Admite que os processos de controle se correlacionem, mas não que a melhora de um deles traga necessariamente a melhora dos outros.
  • (  )Acrescenta uma dimensão que os demais ignoram: se as línguas são usadas em ambientes separados, com interlocutores diferentes ou misturadas na mesma conversa.
  • (  )Põe no centro da função executiva a capacidade de conter uma resposta predominante ou de ignorar informação que concorre com o objetivo.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
1º: Tavares-Lund (4): ‘a multidimensional continuum of experience’, on which individuals are located by age of acquisition, proficiency in each language and the proportion of daily life conducted in each (§5). 2º: Szabo-Ferreira (3): ‘those who use two or more languages, or dialects, in their everyday lives’, a definition which makes regular use, rather than level of mastery, the criterion (§5). 3º: Okonkwo-Lindahl (1): ‘correlated but separable’, so that an improvement in one need not be accompanied by an improvement in the others (§3). 4º: Ibekwe-Castell (5): adds a dimension the others ignore: the interactional context (§5). 5º: Draven-Saito (2): treating inhibitory control as the core of executive function e ‘the ability to withhold a prepotent response or to ignore information that competes with the goal’ (§3).

Armadilhas: Tavares-Lund e Ibekwe-Castell falam ambos em dimensões do bilinguismo, mas só Ibekwe-Castell trata do contexto de interação. Okonkwo-Lindahl também menciona a inibição (the suppression of dominant but inappropriate responses), mas como um de três componentes; quem a põe no centro é Draven-Saito. Szabo-Ferreira e Tavares-Lund tratam ambos do uso diário, mas só Tavares-Lund o combina com idade de aquisição e proficiência.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 5; (c) erra os itens 3 e 4; (d) erra os itens 1 e 2.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em associação de autores, ache em cada definição o elemento que só ela tem (o “centro” da função executiva, o contexto de interação, o uso sem exigência de domínio) e compare com as paráfrases. Autores do mesmo parágrafo costumam ser trocados entre si; resolva pelo menos três itens antes de marcar.

questoes.enunciado:
Indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresenta o parágrafo 6.

  • (  )No levantamento de 118 estudos, menos da metade informava em que idade a segunda língua havia sido adquirida.
  • (  )Segundo Petrakis-Ndlovu (2019), 29 dos estudos analisados classificavam os participantes com base em uma única pergunta de autorrelato.
  • (  )Entre os integrantes de alguns grupos tidos como monolíngues havia quem tivesse estudado outra língua na escola durante seis anos ou mais.
  • (  )Para Petrakis-Ndlovu (2019), quando dois estudos chegam a conclusões opostas, isso se deve ao fato de terem medido populações diferentes.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – D – A – D
A – A – D – A
D – A – D – A
D – D – A – D
A – A – A – D
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): only 41 reported the age at which the second language had been acquired; 41 de 118 é menos da metade (cerca de 35%). A paráfrase troca o número por uma proporção.

2 (D): 29 é o número de estudos com an objective measure of proficiency. Os que usavam uma única pergunta de autorrelato são the remainder, o restante. O número está na mesma frase, por isso a troca é tentadora.

3 (A): Several ‘monolingual’ groups included participants who had studied a second language at school for six years or more.

4 (D): duas trocas. O texto diz que é impossível saber se os estudos divergem sobre o efeito ou se medem populações diferentes (it is therefore impossible to know whether…): é uma dúvida, não uma explicação afirmada. E a frase é dos autores do artigo, não de Petrakis-Ndlovu, a quem se atribui só a conclusão sobre recodificar os dados.

Nas alternativas erradas: (b) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (c) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (d) erra o item 1; (e) erra o item 2.
questoes.dica: Dica: Nos itens de A/D com números, leia a oração inteira em volta de cada número para saber o que ele conta. Desconfie também de itens que transformam uma alternativa “ou isto ou aquilo” em causa afirmada, ou que atribuem a um autor citado o comentário dos autores do artigo.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos sublinhados nos trechos a seguir.

I - “[…] 63% of those reporting a clear advantage had subsequently been published in full […]” (§10)II - “[…] a pattern which is expected when significant results are selectively published […]” (§10)III - “Morland-Achebe (2014) showed that, in a sample of 1,240 primary-school children, […]” (§11)IV - “[…] once parental education and immigrant generation were entered as covariates […]” (§11)

Os segmentos sublinhados estão, respectivamente, nos seguintes tempos e vozes verbais
alternativas: passado perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz ativa – passado simples, voz ativa – passado perfeito, voz passiva.
presente perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz passiva – passado simples, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva.
passado perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz passiva – passado simples, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva.
passado perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva – passado simples, voz passiva.
passado simples, voz passiva – presente simples, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva – passado contínuo, voz passiva.
questoes.explicacao:
I – had subsequently been published: had + been + particípio (published) = passado perfeito, voz passiva. O advérbio subsequently entre os auxiliares não muda a forma. O passado perfeito marca que a publicação aconteceu antes de outro momento passado (a auditoria de Kessling e Yuen). O presente perfeito seria have/has been published, e o passado simples passivo, were published.

II – is expected: is + particípio = presente simples, voz passiva. O sujeito (a pattern) não espera nada; ele é esperado (por quem analisa os dados, agente omitido). Na voz ativa seria algo como which researchers expect.

III – showed: verbo simples no passado, sem be + particípio = passado simples, voz ativa. O sujeito Morland-Achebe (2014) pratica a ação de mostrar. A forma no passado não indica passiva; a passiva seria it was shown.

IV – were entered: were + particípio = passado simples, voz passiva: as variáveis foram inseridas como covariáveis (por quem fez a análise). O passado contínuo exigiria -ing (were being entered), e o passado perfeito, had been entered.

Logo, (c). As outras: (a) erra II (lê is expected como ativa) e IV (vê um passado perfeito sem had); (b) erra I, confundindo had been com has been; (d) erra II e III (toma o -ed/passado de showed por passiva); (e) erra os quatro itens.
questoes.dica: Dica: Procure be + particípio: se houver, é voz passiva, e o tempo é o do auxiliar be (is → presente simples; were → passado simples; has been → presente perfeito; had been → passado perfeito; is/were being → contínuo). Sem be + particípio, é voz ativa, mesmo que o verbo esteja no passado. Advérbios entre os auxiliares (subsequently, also) não mudam a análise.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado indica que os autores consideram algo IMPROVÁVEL, isto é, pouco provável de acontecer ou de ser verdade.
alternativas: “[…] in other settings bilingual children more often come from low-income households, which <u>would be expected to</u> mask any advantage rather than produce one” (§11).
“These components are, in her account, ‘correlated but separable’, so that an improvement in one <u>need not</u> be accompanied by an improvement in the others” (§3).
“[…] a speaker in a dense code-switching community, where mixing is the norm, <u>may</u> need comparatively little inhibition at all” (§16).
“A speaker who uses each language in a separate setting […] rarely needs to switch within a conversation and <u>should</u> therefore make modest demands on inhibition” (§16).
“A measure that does not correlate with itself across two sessions <u>is unlikely to</u> correlate with language background” (§4).
questoes.explicacao:
Is unlikely to (“é improvável que”) avalia como baixa a probabilidade de algo ser verdade: uma medida que nem se correlaciona consigo mesma dificilmente se correlacionará com o histórico linguístico → (e).

(a) would be expected to indica o contrário: algo provável, esperado (a baixa renda tenderia a encobrir a vantagem). (b) need not é a armadilha da forma negativa: expressa ausência de necessidade (“não precisa”, “não necessariamente”), e não baixa probabilidade. (c) may indica possibilidade, sem dizer se ela é alta ou baixa. (d) should, aqui, não é recomendação: com therefore, expressa uma expectativa razoável, algo provável. O rarely da mesma frase fala de frequência (“raramente precisa alternar”), não do grau de certeza dos autores, e por isso também engana.
questoes.dica: Dica: Separe probabilidade de necessidade. Probabilidade alta: will, would be expected to, should (expectativa), is likely to; baixa: is unlikely to, is hardly to be expected, there is little chance that; neutra: may, might, could. Need not e do not have to falam de necessidade (“não precisa”), e advérbios de frequência (rarely, seldom) falam de quantas vezes algo acontece.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale o segmento que NÃO inclui relação lógica de CONSEQUÊNCIA entre as ideias.
alternativas: “Their limitation is that switch costs depend heavily on the interval between cue and stimulus, so that laboratories using different intervals may obtain results that cannot be compared” (§19).
“Even so, the findings were consistent with a coherent theoretical account, and their consistency was taken as corroboration” (§9).
“Where two studies reach opposite conclusions, it is therefore impossible to know whether they disagree about the effect of bilingualism or are simply measuring different populations” (§6).
“[…] and two studies of ‘balanced bilinguals’ may accordingly be studying quite different people” (§7).
“The debate has consequently reached a form of impasse” (§14).
questoes.explicacao:
(b) começa com Even so (“mesmo assim”, “ainda assim”), que marca concessão: apesar da cautela que amostras pequenas deveriam ter inspirado, os achados foram aceitos. O so dentro da expressão é a armadilha; sozinho, so pode indicar consequência, mas even so não. O and que vem depois só soma uma informação.

As demais trazem consequência: (a) so that (“de modo que”): por dependerem do intervalo, os resultados de laboratórios diferentes não se comparam; (c) therefore (“portanto”), mesmo no meio da oração; (d) accordingly (“em consequência”, “por conseguinte”): como os limiares variam, os estudos podem estar tratando de pessoas diferentes; (e) consequently.
questoes.dica: Dica: Procure o conector em qualquer posição da frase, não só no início (therefore, accordingly e consequently aparecem no meio). Conectores de consequência: so, so that, therefore, thus, consequently, accordingly, as a result. Cuidado com expressões que contêm essas palavras mas mudam de sentido: even so (concessão), so far (tempo), not so much… as (comparação).

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “Proponents objected that their participants had been classified by a single question and tested on home computers, under conditions that could not be controlled. These objections were partly met by Lindholm-Amaro (2018), who tested 486 children in schools using identical equipment and a detailed language-background interview, and who also reported no reliable effect” (§12) e “[…] the pooled effect was close to zero, and its confidence interval excluded the values reported in the studies […]” (§12) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: Proponents – a ausência de diferença entre os grupos em todas as medidas – 486 children – the pooled effect.
Varhaug, Szalai e Osei (2015) – a testagem em computadores domésticos, em condições que não podiam ser controladas – 486 children – Two subsequent meta-analyses.
Proponents – as críticas à classificação dos participantes por uma única pergunta e à testagem em computadores domésticos – 486 children – the pooled effect.
Varhaug, Szalai e Osei (2015) – as críticas à classificação dos participantes por uma única pergunta e à testagem em computadores domésticos – Lindholm-Amaro (2018) – the pooled effect.
Varhaug, Szalai e Osei (2015) – as críticas à classificação dos participantes por uma única pergunta e à testagem em computadores domésticos – Lindholm-Amaro (2018) – Two subsequent meta-analyses.
questoes.explicacao:
their: os participantes eram os do estudo criticado, isto é, de Varhaug, Szalai e Osei (2015), sujeito da frase anterior. Proponents é o substantivo plural mais próximo, mas os defensores da hipótese não tinham participantes: eles fizeram a objeção ao estudo dos outros.

These objections: o plural resume as duas críticas da frase anterior: a classificação por uma única pergunta e a testagem em computadores domésticos sem controle. Ficar só com a segunda, a mais próxima, deixa de fora metade do referente; a frase seguinte confirma, porque Lindholm-Amaro responde às duas (identical equipment e a detailed language-background interview). A ausência de diferença é o resultado criticado, não a crítica.

who: o segundo who está coordenado ao primeiro por and (who tested … and who also reported) e tem o mesmo antecedente, Lindholm-Amaro (2018). 486 children é o substantivo de pessoa mais próximo, mas as crianças foram testadas; quem relata um efeito é o pesquisador.

its: possessivo singular. Two subsequent meta-analyses é plural (pediria their); o intervalo de confiança é do efeito combinado (the pooled effect), sujeito da oração anterior.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2 e 3; (b) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (c) erra os itens 1 e 3; (e) erra o item 4.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para cada pronome, confira número (it/its × they/their) e teste o candidato no lugar dele (“os participantes dos defensores?”). Em this/these + substantivo, veja quantas ideias anteriores o substantivo resume. Um who coordenado por and a outro who tem o mesmo antecedente que o primeiro, mesmo que haja substantivos no meio.

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “Each reply is reasonable in itself, but each was formulated after the repeated failure of large, internet-based samples of young adults to reproduce the laboratory findings, and none specifies in advance the result that would count against it” (§13) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: o fracasso repetido de grandes amostras de jovens adultos, coletadas pela internet, em reproduzir os achados de laboratório.
o fracasso dos achados de laboratório em reproduzir, repetidas vezes, grandes amostras de jovens adultos coletadas pela internet.
as grandes amostras repetidas de jovens adultos, coletadas pela internet, que fracassaram em reproduzir os achados de laboratório.
o fracasso repetido de jovens adultos em reproduzir, em grandes amostras pela internet, os achados de laboratório.
a falha repetida em reproduzir, com grandes amostras de laboratório, os achados obtidos pela internet com jovens adultos.
questoes.explicacao:
O núcleo é failure (fracasso), qualificado por repeated. Ele tem dois complementos: of large, internet-based samples of young adults diz de quem é o fracasso (de grandes amostras de jovens adultos, baseadas na internet), e a oração de infinitivo to reproduce the laboratory findings diz em quê (em reproduzir os achados de laboratório). É a estrutura the failure of X to do Y = “o fracasso de X em fazer Y”.

(b) inverte X e Y: faz dos achados o sujeito do fracasso. (c) troca o núcleo para samples e faz repeated modificar as amostras. (d) põe os jovens adultos como quem fracassa; eles são os participantes das amostras. (e) troca de lugar internet e laboratory: as amostras é que são da internet, e os achados, de laboratório.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em “the + substantivo + of X + to + verbo” (the failure of X to…, the tendency of X to…, the ability of X to…), X é quem pratica a ação do infinitivo. Traduza o núcleo, depois “de X”, depois “em/a + verbo”. Os adjetivos antes do substantivo (large, internet-based) ficam com o substantivo que vem logo depois deles.

questoes.enunciado: A função do segmento destacado em “Studies that define bilingualism more carefully have also tended to be larger and better matched. Paradoxically, it is these studies, which ought to have been best placed to reveal an advantage if one existed, that have most consistently failed to find it” (§14) é
alternativas: introduzir uma ressalva que restringe a afirmação anterior de que os estudos mais cuidadosos foram também maiores e mais bem pareados.
apresentar como consequência lógica da frase anterior o fato de esses estudos não terem encontrado a vantagem.
assinalar que o resultado relatado contraria o que seria de esperar, dadas as qualidades desses estudos.
marcar a oposição entre a posição dos defensores da hipótese e a dos críticos, apresentada no início do parágrafo.
enfatizar que os estudos mais cuidadosos foram justamente os que mais vezes confirmaram a vantagem bilíngue.
questoes.explicacao:
Paradoxically (“paradoxalmente”) anuncia um fato que contraria a expectativa. A própria frase explica qual era a expectativa: esses estudos ought to have been best placed to reveal an advantage if one existed (deveriam ser os mais capazes de revelar a vantagem, se ela existisse), e no entanto have most consistently failed to find it → (c).

(a) a frase anterior não é limitada nem corrigida: continua valendo que os estudos cuidadosos foram maiores e mais bem pareados; é justamente isso que torna o resultado paradoxal. (b) não há consequência: de estudos maiores e mais bem pareados se esperaria o contrário (encontrar a vantagem). (d) a oposição entre defensores e críticos está no início do parágrafo, mas é feita por and e pelo paralelismo, não por Paradoxically. (e) inverte o conteúdo: esses estudos foram os que mais vezes não encontraram a vantagem (de 58% para 17% de comparações favoráveis).
questoes.dica: Dica: Advérbios de comentário no início da frase (paradoxically, ironically, surprisingly, predictably) dizem como o autor avalia o fato, não como ele se liga à frase anterior. Para identificar a função, pergunte qual era a expectativa e se o fato a confirma ou a contraria.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere as seguintes afirmações sobre a técnica denominada Language-background questionnaires (§20).

I - Permitem tratar o bilinguismo como um conjunto de variáveis contínuas, e não como uma categoria, e, quando o mesmo instrumento é aplicado em vários estudos, tornam comparáveis resultados de populações diferentes.II - No estudo de Ibekwe-Castell (2016), as estimativas da proporção do tempo passado em cada língua foram, em média, o dobro das obtidas a partir da fala gravada.III - Nos instrumentos mais bem construídos, a proficiência não é apenas autoavaliada pelos participantes, mas também testada.IV - Os escores que produzem têm baixa confiabilidade e se correlacionam fracamente entre si, o que põe em dúvida se medem uma capacidade comum.

Estão em acordo com o texto
alternativas: apenas I e IV.
apenas I e III.
apenas I, II e III.
apenas III e IV.
apenas II e IV.
questoes.explicacao:
I (acordo): they allow bilingualism to be treated as a set of continuous variables rather than as a category and, when the same instrument is used across studies, make results from different populations comparable.

II (desacordo): o que foi inflado por um fator de dois foi a frequência diária de alternância (estimates of daily switching frequency were inflated by a factor of two on average); a proporção do tempo em cada língua foi estimada com razoável precisão (were reasonably accurate). O item troca os dois tipos de estimativa.

III (acordo): self-rated and, in better instruments, tested proficiency.

IV (desacordo): é verdade no texto, mas sobre outra técnica: a baixa confiabilidade do escore de interferência e a correlação fraca entre as duas tarefas (r = .12) são limitações de Flanker and Simon tasks (§18).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) inclui IV e deixa de fora III; (c) inclui II; (d) inclui IV e deixa de fora I; (e) inclui II e IV e deixa de fora I e III.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em afirmações I, II, III sobre uma seção, confira de que seção veio cada informação (a limitação de uma técnica vizinha costuma aparecer como item) e, nos itens com dois tipos de dado, veja a qual deles o número se aplica. Concessões com although no fim da frase costumam guardar a informação que o item inverte.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “participants alternate between two simple tasks […] according to a cue that changes unpredictably” (§19)II - “estimates of the proportion of time spent in each language were reasonably accurate” (§20)III - “A practical compromise, lately adopted in several studies, is to combine a short questionnaire with language diaries” (§20)IV - “a number that laboratories testing in person can seldom reach” (§21)

Os segmentos sublinhados apresentam, respectivamente, ideia de
alternativas: frequência – modo – modo – tempo.
modo – intensidade – modo – frequência.
tempo – intensidade – tempo – tempo.
modo – modo – tempo – tempo.
modo – intensidade – tempo – frequência.
questoes.explicacao:
I unpredictably = “de forma imprevisível”: diz como a pista muda → modo. Não é frequência (a): o advérbio não diz quantas vezes a pista muda, e sim de que maneira (sem que o participante possa prever). Também não é tempo (c): não situa a mudança num momento.

II reasonably = “razoavelmente”, “bastante”: gradua o quanto as estimativas eram precisas → intensidade. Modifica o adjetivo accurate, não um verbo; apesar do -ly, não descreve uma maneira de agir, por isso não é modo (a, d).

III lately = “recentemente”, “ultimamente”: situa no tempo a adoção do meio-termo → tempo. É um -ly que não indica modo (a, b): não significa “com atraso” (late) nem diz como o meio-termo foi adotado.

IV seldom = “raramente”: diz com que frequência os laboratórios conseguem atingir esse número → frequência, não tempo (a, c, d), pois não situa a ação num momento, e sim quantas vezes ela ocorre.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens I, II, III e IV; (b) erra o item III; (c) erra os itens I e IV; (d) erra os itens II e IV.
questoes.dica: Dica: classifique o advérbio pela pergunta que ele responde no trecho: como? (modo), em que grau? (intensidade: reasonably, largely, fairly), quando? (tempo: lately, formerly, now), com que frequência? (seldom, rarely, routinely). O sufixo -ly não garante modo, e “quando” é diferente de “quantas vezes”.

questoes.enunciado:
Associe as colunas de modo a indicar o que cada segmento está fazendo no texto.

  1. Sugerindo
  2. Questionando
  3. Exemplificando
  4. Ressalvando
  5. Citando outro autor
  • (  )“‘Functional bilingual’, for instance, is defined in one widely used protocol simply as ‘a person who can function in two languages’” (§7)
  • (  )“If no conceivable result could count against them, in what sense do they remain empirical claims?” (§13)
  • (  )“Early tests are encouraging but small.” (§16)
  • (  )“Laboratories might usefully agree on a small set of standard intervals […]” (§19)

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
1º (3, exemplificando): for instance anuncia um caso concreto da afirmação anterior, Some accounts, however, offer no explanation of how the new label differs from the old (§7): o rótulo functional bilingual ilustra essa falha. O trecho reproduz a definição de um protocolo, mas não atribui uma ideia a um autor; a função dele no parágrafo é dar o exemplo. Por isso, 5 (citando outro autor) é a leitura apressada.

2º (2, questionando): é uma pergunta retórica (in what sense…?). Ela põe em dúvida o caráter empírico das três réplicas dos defensores da hipótese, que none specifies in advance the result that would count against it (§13). Não sugere nenhuma ação nem dá exemplo.

3º (4, ressalvando): encouraging but small reconhece um ponto positivo e logo o limita com but: os primeiros testes da abordagem contextual são animadores, porém pequenos (§16). Não cita ninguém; a referência a Haverkamp-Iwu (2021) vem na frase seguinte. Logo, 5 está errado nessa posição.

4º (1, sugerindo): might usefully agree propõe uma medida aos laboratórios: padronizar os intervalos entre pista e estímulo (§19). O modal might com usefully marca sugestão, não ressalva nem pergunta.

Sequência 3 – 2 – 4 – 1 → (a). (b) e (c) tomam o exemplo do §7 por citação de autor; (c) ainda inverte pergunta e exemplo e põe “ressalvando” na sugestão; (d) toma a ressalva do §16 por citação; (e) troca a função de todos os segmentos.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para dizer o que um segmento está fazendo, procure as marcas da função: for instance, such as, e.g. (exemplificar); pergunta direta ou whether (questionar); but, although, however, yet logo depois de uma avaliação positiva (ressalvar); might/could usefully, should, it would be advisable (sugerir); Segundo X (ano), X argues (citar outro autor). Confira a função no parágrafo, não só as palavras do trecho.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que apresenta uma informação FALSA de acordo com o texto.
alternativas: Segundo Feldt-Arango (2020), os efeitos de interferência de quatro tarefas comuns tiveram correlações teste-reteste entre 0,20 e 0,45, bem abaixo das dos tempos de resposta globais (§4).
Nos primeiros estudos sobre a hipótese, as amostras raramente passavam de 40 participantes por grupo, e eram frequentes diferenças padronizadas de 0,6 ou mais (§9).
Como os resumos haviam sido aceitos nos mesmos congressos, dificilmente a diferença entre as taxas de publicação se explicaria por diferenças de qualidade (§10).
Em 1.240 crianças, a vantagem de d = 0,25 na tarefa flanker sumiu ao se controlarem a escolaridade dos pais e a geração de imigração, e também a idade e o sexo (§11).
Detectar com poder adequado um efeito de d = 0,10 exigiria mais de 1.500 participantes por grupo, número que raramente se alcança em testagem presencial (§21).
questoes.explicacao:
(d) é a falsa. A primeira metade está certa, mas o texto diz o oposto sobre idade e sexo: a vantagem disappeared once parental education and immigrant generation were entered as covariates, whereas it was unaffected by controlling for age and sex (§11). Whereas contrasta os dois controles; a alternativa os soma (“e também”).

As outras são verdadeiras, só parafraseadas. (a): test–retest correlations between .20 and .45 for the interference effects of four commonly used tasks, against .80 or more for the overall response times (§4). (b): Effect sizes in this early literature were frequently large, with standardised differences of 0.6 or more, and samples rarely exceeded 40 participants per group (§9). (c): Because the abstracts had been accepted at the same meetings, differences in quality could not easily explain the gap (§10). (e): a study large enough to detect an effect of d = 0.10 with adequate power requires more than 1,500 participants per group, a number that laboratories testing in person can seldom reach (§21).
questoes.dica: Dica: Em “assinale a FALSA”, confira cada alternativa parte por parte no parágrafo indicado: números, quantificadores (raramente, frequentes, mais de), quem fez o quê e conectores. A falsa costuma ter a maior parte certa e trocar um único detalhe, como somar o que o texto contrasta (whereas, while) ou inverter uma condição.

questoes.enunciado: Qual alternativa sintetiza a CONCLUSÃO (§23–§24) a que chegam os autores?
alternativas: Como os estudos maiores e mais controlados não encontraram a vantagem em jovens adultos, a experiência linguística não tem consequências para o controle cognitivo.
Perguntar se bilíngues têm melhor controle executivo é grosseiro demais; cabe perguntar que experiências, em que contextos, se associam a que componentes do controle.
A vantagem bilíngue se restringe a crianças e idosos, já que, nos jovens adultos, o desempenho nas tarefas de conflito está próximo do teto.
O rótulo “vantagem bilíngue” deve ser substituído por um termo mais preciso, que delimite o subgrupo de falantes em que o efeito é esperado.
Por serem pouco confiáveis, as tarefas de conflito devem dar lugar a questionários de histórico linguístico nas pesquisas futuras.
questoes.explicacao:
(b) resume o §24: a pergunta deve ser reformulada because, in its present form, it is too coarse to be answered, e a pesquisa deve perguntar which features of language experience, in which contexts of use, are associated with which components of control.

(a) a primeira metade está certa (§23), mas a conclusão tirada é a que o texto nega: It does not, however, demonstrate that language experience has no consequences for cognitive control. (c) para crianças e idosos a evidência remains inconclusive; o efeito teto é uma das réplicas dos defensores (§13), não a conclusão. (d) contradiz The need is not for a new label for the advantage. (e) os autores pedem as duas coisas: medir o bilinguismo como experiências contínuas e o controle executivo with tasks of known reliability; não substituem uma pela outra.
questoes.dica: Dica: Leia a conclusão inteira e procure as frases com not… but (“não X, mas Y”) e however: elas dizem o que os autores rejeitam. Distratores costumam juntar uma premissa verdadeira a uma conclusão que o texto recusa, ou apresentar como tese a posição de outro grupo citado no meio do artigo.
